units.text: 22. A protocol for a suspicious world

Return to the prologue’s clocks. The ratio between two frequencies starts changing. One team announces an error. Another, an unknown physical field. A third, intervention in the simulation. How do we organize research so that more than the story with the best headline can win?

First we specify the phenomenon. Not ‘time runs differently’, but a particular dimensionless ratio between two transition types, measured through an identifiable protocol, deviates from a model by a certain magnitude and temporal structure. Choosing the ratio prevents a mere unit change from being confused with changed physics. Research on varying constants uses precisely comparisons where physical dependencies and model assumptions are explicit (Uzan, 2011) .

Then we formulate sufficiently concrete competing explanations. One model describes thermal drift in the instrument. Another, a synchronization-chain problem. A third introduces a field affecting the two mechanisms differently. A fourth proposes a discrete modification of an implementation rule. The list need not be complete; we must not treat our preferred model as the sole alternative to standard theory.

For each explanation we ask what else should change. Does the effect appear in every instrument or only one batch? Does it depend on temperature, position, material or software version? Does it have the same form in laboratories sharing neither instruments nor code? Independence means more than multiple addresses. Ten teams using the same faulty library can perfectly reproduce the same mistake.

Predictions must be recorded before choosing the data they will evaluate. If we examine thousands of frequencies, periods and directions and report only the unusual combination, chance can acquire the appearance of law. We separate exploration from confirmation: find a pattern in one observation set, then put it at risk on new data. We also retain negative results. Such practices address a general research problem: incentives for publishable results do not automatically coincide with incentives for true results (Nosek, Spies și Motyl, 2012) .

The intervention model must also pay the price of precision. ‘Someone changes anything, anytime, however they want’ offers no determinate probability of observations. A table of exceptions invented after the result can reproduce any history. By contrast, a hypothesis specifying a particular class of modifications and predicting as-yet unmeasured relationships can be compared with rivals. It need not claim to explain everything to deserve testing.

We can build a small research program without waiting for a cosmic anomaly. The project proposed here would begin with artificial worlds whose mechanisms are known only to the evaluator. We do not claim this experiment has been conducted. Its purpose would be to test whether our methods distinguish possible causes of a change before applying them to the universe.

In the first family, rules remain fixed but the observer sees only collective variables. In the second, a regime change brings other effective relationships into view. In the third, an internal parameter evolves under a stable rule. In the fourth, the evaluator modifies a rule externally. In the fifth, the world does not change at all: the sensor or processing software fails. The observer receives the same interface types and a comparable experimental budget.

The difficulty must be constructed correctly. If every external intervention is abrupt and every internal process smooth, an algorithm will learn the distinction we artificially chose. Internal jumps, slow external interventions and errors resembling both must be included. The mechanism’s true label must not be guessable from a data-generator artifact.

Evaluation occurs on new worlds, not merely new rows from the same worlds. Otherwise the method may memorize a simulator’s peculiarities and seem to discover general principles. We compare the detector with simple methods and measure false alarms, detection delay and the proportion of cases where it justifiably refuses to decide. Saying ‘these two explanations cannot be separated by the available data’ may be an epistemic success, not a failure.

We deliberately introduce pairs of observationally equivalent worlds as well. In one, a hidden variable changes the dynamics; in the other, the evaluator externally applies exactly the same change. If interfaces produce the same observations under every permitted intervention, no detector should reliably distinguish them. A system announcing certainty in such a situation has not overcome the theoretical limit. Most likely it exploited an information leak or evaluation error.

This laboratory would produce useful results even if it showed how little we can identify. We would learn which new experiments reduce ambiguity, which conclusions depend on hidden-variable access and when classification must be replaced with a set of compatible explanations. In an AI program for scientific discovery, the ability to declare underdetermination should be evaluated alongside the ability to find formulas.

For real observations, the next step would be a public register of predictions, protocols and data, with independent checks and explicit stopping rules. A campaign’s result must be formulated at the level it supports: ‘this model class is incompatible with the data in this domain’, ‘there is an unreproduced deviation’, or ‘the new model predicts these observations better’. None of these statements should automatically become ‘we found the programmer’.

There is also a mundane but important ethical limit: no simulation hypothesis justifies causing disasters to force the system to ‘react’. Experiments must meet the same safety requirements as other research. A method claiming to test reality by sacrificing people already starts from a moral conclusion the data cannot authorize.

The program is useful because it shifts emphasis from fascination to discrimination. The question is no longer whether we can tell a plausible story after seeing a change. It is whether we can anticipate which observation would distinguish two mechanisms and honestly acknowledge cases where no accessible observation distinguishes them.
